## Background

All functions in R have at least 3 things:

- a *name* (we pick that and use it to call the function)
- input *arguments* (one or more comma separated inputs that go inside the brackets when we call the function)
- the *body* (the lines of R code that do the work of the function)

## A first function

Here we will create a function `add()` to add numbers together.

> **Q1a.** Your first version of the function should add two input numbers together. For example, add(4,7) should return 11. \[1 pt\]

```{r}
add <- function(x, y=0) {
  x + y
}
```

Let's test our new function

```{r}
add (4, 7)
```

```{r}
add (10)
```

```{r}
add <- function(x, y=0, z) {
  x + y + z
}
```

```{r}
add (10,10,100)
```

> **Q1b.** For you second version, adapt your first function so it can take a single input vector or two inputs as before. For example, add(4, 7) and add( c(4,7,10) ). \[1 pt\]

```{r}
add <- function(x, y=0) {
  sum (x,y)
}
```

```{r}
add ( c(4,7) )
```

> **Q1c.** c. Finally, on your own (outside of class) create a third version of your function that can add any number of inputs that the user provides. For example, add(1, 2, 3, -4) should return 2. Hint: explore the ... (dots) argument or the base R function sum(). \[2 pts\]

```{r}

add(1, 2, 3, -4)
```

## Generate a DNA function

Write a function generate_dna() that returns a random DNA sequence of a length specified by the user.

> **Q2a.** Your first version should return a multi-element vector of single character nucleotides. For example generate_dna(6) might return "A", "T", "T", "G", "A", "C". \[1 pt\]

Useful base R functions that you may (or may not) find useful for this lab include: `sample()`, `paste()`, `paste0()`, `if()`, `for()`, `sapply()`, `nchar()`, and `cat()`.

The `sample()` looks useful. There are two **required** arguments (i.e., inputs I must give that don't have a default value)

```{r}
sample (x=1:10, size=3) 
```

We can use this with "A" "C" "G" "T" as input x to generate a random nucleotide sequence

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(len)
  sample (x=c("A", "C", "T", "G"), size = len, replace = TRUE) 
```

We now have a working snippet of code that does something useful. This can serve as the "body" of our first `generate_dna()` function.

```{r}
generate_dna(6)
```

> **Q2b.** Your second version should optionally be able to return either a multi-element vector of single character nucleotides (as before) or a single character string (not a vector of single letters but a singe vector of multiple letters). For example "AAGGCTG". \[1 pt\]

```{r}
paste ( c("A", "C", "A"), collapse = "")
```

```{r}
flag <- TRUE
if (flag) {
  cat ("Look at me! We are in here")
} else {
  cat ("NOooo")
}
```

Let's combine these two things into our new improved function:

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(len, collapse = FALSE){

  # Multi-element nucleotide vector
  s <- sample (x=c("A", "C", "T", "G"), size = len, replace = TRUE)
 
  # create an if argument
  if (collapse) {
    
  # Make a single element vector 
  s <- paste (s, collapse = "")
  }
  return (s)
}

```

```{r}
generate_dna(6, collapse = T)
generate_dna(6, collapse = F)
generate_dna(6)
```

> **Q2c.** Finally, create a final version of your function that prints out a FASTA format sequence with an id line indicating the sequence length.

```{r}
len <- 9
paste(">length", len, sep = "")
```

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(len, FASTA = FALSE){

  # Multi-element nucleotide vector
  s <- sample (x=c("A", "C", "T", "G"), size = len, replace = TRUE)
 
  # create an if argument
  if (FASTA) {
    
  # Make a single element vector
    
  s <- paste (s, collapse = "")
  
    # Add a FASTA ID 
  
  id <- paste(">length", len, sep = "")
  s <- paste (id, s, sep = "\n")
  cat(s)
  }
  return (s)
}
```

```{r}
x <- generate_dna(9, FASTA = T)
```

## Write a `generate_protein()`function

Write a function generate_protein() that returns a random peptide/protein sequence of a length specified by the user. For example generate_protein(6) might return "WQRTAG". Your function should:

> Use the single-letter code for all 20 standard amino acids and no other letters and include clear comments that explain each step of your function. \[2 pts\]

```{r}
generate_protein <- function(len, FASTA = FALSE){

  # Multi-element amino acids
  s <- sample (x=c("A", "R", "N", "D", "C", "E", "Q", "G", "H", "I", "L", "K", "M", "F", "P", "S","T", "W", "Y", "V"), size = len, replace = TRUE)
 
  # create an if argument
  if (FASTA) {
    
  # Make a single element vector 
  s <- paste (s, collapse = "")
  }
  return (s)
}

```

```{r}
generate_protein(6, FASTA = TRUE)
```

## Generate random protein sequences of length 6 to 13

Adapt and use your generate_protein() function to generate a series of random protein sequences ranging from 6 to 13 amino acids in length (one sequence per length). Take advantage of the base R function for() or sapply() so that you do not have to call generate_protein() eight times by hand.

Be sure to format your results in FASTA format ready to paste or upload as a query to NCBI BLASTp

```{r}
generate_protein <- function(len, FASTA = FALSE) {
  
  # The 20 standard amino acids (single-letter codes)
  amino_acids <- c("A", "R", "N", "D", "C", "E", "Q", "G", "H", "I",
                   "L", "K", "M", "F", "P", "S", "T", "W", "Y", "V")
  
  # Randomly pick 'len' amino acids, allowing repeats
  s <- sample(x = amino_acids, size = len, replace = TRUE)
  
  # Join the letters into a single string
  s <- paste(s, collapse = "")
  
  # Add a FASTA header line with the sequence length
  if (FASTA) {
    s <- paste0(">id.", len, "\n", s)
  }
  
  return(s)
}
```

```{r}

#We can do this with a `for()` loop
for (len in 6:13) {
  
  #Generate protein sequence
  cat(generate_protein(len, FASTA = TRUE), "\n")
}
```

```{r}
sapply(6:13, generate_protein, FASTA = T)

 #Generate protein sequence
  cat(generate_protein(len, FASTA = TRUE), "\n")
```

## BLASTp search against nr — are your peptides “unique in nature”?

Take your FASTA-formatted peptides from Q4 and run them as a single BLASTp search against the **Non-redundant protein sequences (nr)** database at https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/.

```{r}
blast_results <- data.frame(
  Length = 6:13,
  Best_Hit_Identity = c(100, 100, 100, 88.89, 90.91, 90.91, 80, 83.33),
  Best_Hit_Coverage = c(100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 83, 92),
  Unique   = c("N", "N", "N", "Y", "Y", "Y", "Y", "Y")
)

blast_results
```

> **Q5a.** At which sequence length do your randomly generated peptides start to look “unique in nature” (i.e. no 100% coverage + 100% identity hit)? \[1 pt\]

At **sequence length 9**, my randomly generated peptides start to look “unique in nature” (88.89% identity, 100% coverage)

> **Q5b.** Speculate why very short random peptides are almost always found in nr, while longer ones typically are not.

Increasing the number of amino acids (AA) increases the number of possible AA combinations exponentially: with 20 amino acids, there are 20ⁿ possible peptides of length n. Because the nr database is large but finite, very short peptides have few possible sequences that almost all of them appear somewhere in nr by chance. As peptide length increases, the number of possible sequences quickly exceeds what exists in nr, so longer random peptides are typically not found.

> **Q6.** In 3–6 sentences total and using your Q5 data and the reasoning from Q5b, what do you think this minimum length is and why might it be a bad design choice for the immune system to present very short peptides? [3 pt]

Based on my data in Q5, the minimum length is 9 amino acids, since my 6–8 aa random peptides all had 100% identity and coverage matches in nr, while peptides of 9 aa and longer did not. A very short peptide from a pathogen would almost cerainly appear in an organism's own proteins, and so the immune system would not able to distinguish self from non-self. This would be a bad and dangerous design choice. If T cells responses to these short peptides, it can result in an autoimmune disease (T cells attacking self), or because T cells that recognize self peptides are eliminated during development, there would be no T cells left to recognize the pathogen, leaving the infection undetected.
